entry.title: fix: offer apps without a bundle id in the target picker (#21)
entry.content:
fix: offer apps without a bundle id in the target picker (#21)

* fix(yomi): list and follow apps that have no bundle id

The picker's --list-all dropped every window whose owner had no bundle id,
on the assumption that "no bundle id" means "not an application". It does
not. A bare executable is still an app with a Dock tile, named after its
binary — and that is what every game run through CrossOver is: Wine names
the process after the .exe and there is no Info.plist to carry an id. The
skip hid all of them from the picker (issue #20). A Launcher made in
CrossOver worked only because it wraps the game in a real .app.

Measured 2026-09-10 with a bare AppKit executable named Game.exe:
NSRunningApplication reports bundleIdentifier nil, localizedName "Game.exe";
--list-all returned 36 windows and none of them. After: 37, one with
bundle "" and app "Game.exe".

The skip now asks the question it meant to ask — is the pid an application
LaunchServices knows at all — which still excludes the window server and
the agents, and stops excluding apps that merely lack an id. The Dock skip
stays.

Following such an app needs a name rather than an id, so --app NAME does
for it what --bundle does for the rest, keyed on the application name SCK
reports. Measured: `--app Game.exe --list` finds the same window --list-all
lists, so the picker's name and SCK's agree. The display-capture fallback's
frontmost check reads the same name from NSWorkspace.

* fix(settings): pick and save an app that has no bundle id

The picker grouped windows by bundle id and saved the choice as one, so an
app that --list-all now reports with bundle "" had no identity to be
grouped or saved under, and yomi had nothing to follow.

A target now carries either a bundle id or, for an app without one, the
name on its Dock tile — the same fallback the helper reports and --app
follows. The picker keys its rows on whichever the window has; config.js
sanitises `app` the way it does `bundle`, labels by it, and hands it to yomi
as --app. Every existing config still reads the same: `app` is null unless
the user chose such a target.

Covered by the settings suite with a Game.exe window beside Safari — chosen,
applied, and saved as {bundle: null, app: 'Game.exe'} — and by config.test.js
for the sanitising.

* test: a bare-executable rig for the target picker

Golden cannot see --list-all, and the settings suite is handed its window
list by the test, so nothing unattended could have caught the picker
dropping apps without a bundle id. verify_picker.py builds the ground truth
instead of faking it: a Mach-O with no Info.plist — the shape of every game
run through CrossOver — opens a window, and the live window server is asked
whether --list-all offers it and whether --app follows it.

Measured: against the helper built from main it fails at step 1; against
this branch both steps pass. YOMI_BIN points it at another build, as in
golden.sh.

* fix(yomi): name a listed app by LaunchServices, not the window server

--list-all named each window's app by kCGWindowOwnerName, which the window
server truncates to 31 bytes — ten kanji. A game whose Dock name is longer
was offered under a cut-off name that --app, which matches the application
name SCK reports, could not resolve: listed, but not followable.

Measured 2026-09-14 on a CrossOver process named 飼い犬勇者と魔王の城.exe:
owner "飼い犬勇者と魔王の城." (31 bytes), NSRunningApplication.localizedName
"飼い犬勇者と魔王の城.exe" (34). `--app` with the first: no matching
windows. With the second: the game's window, id 44733.

The pid → NSRunningApplication map was already there for the bundle id;
the name now comes from the same place, so the picker shows the name yomi
follows. The rig's name is now longer than 31 bytes, so verify_picker.py
fails on the old code — the old "Rig.exe" fit and matched both ways.

entry.title: feat: deinflect adjectives too, and drop the last GPL dependency (#16)
entry.content:
feat: deinflect adjectives too, and drop the last GPL dependency (#16)

* chore: vendor jp-verbs, an MIT deinflection table

The app ships no runtime node_modules — build-release.sh copies app/vendor/
into the bundle and nothing else — so a dependency has to be vendored to
exist at runtime. Same arrangement the Yomitan tables have.

Verbatim jp-verbs 1.1.0 apart from one line, recorded with its measurements
in PROVENANCE.md: ADJECTIVE joins the word types that count as a finished
deinflection. The table already carries 44 adjective rules and upstream walks
all of them, then discards every result, because the package is about verbs.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat: deinflect adjectives too, and drop the last GPL dependency

The deinflector was Yomitan's japanese-transforms.js, vendored under GPL-3.0,
which made the whole app a GPL derivative work. Swapped for the jp-verbs table
added in the previous commit: MIT, no lexicon, same prefix-in / candidates-out
shape, so lookup() is unchanged around it.

What the reader gets: adjectives. 高くない, 高かった, 高くなかった and 高ければ
all deinflected to nothing before and answer 高い now — the old table covered
them, but this one covers them and the popup asks for them the same way.

What it costs, measured on 転生してきた僕は信じられている, a full prefix scan:
40 unique candidates against Yomitan's 29, 0.19 ms against 0.10 ms. The extra
candidates are junk like 信じらる that no dictionary has, so each is one
indexed probe that returns nothing. Both numbers are far under one OCR pass.

initTransformer() goes with it. It existed because japanese-transforms.js is
ESM and had to be awaited before the first hover could arrive; jp-verbs is
CommonJS, so the require is the load. That also takes ~4 s off the node suite.

Route steps are renamed rather than lost: jp-verbs names a step for a reader
("ている・でいる Continuing State/Result"), and the popup wants a caption, so
shortStep() keeps the Japanese and drops the English gloss.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* chore: drop vendor files the app never loads, refresh stale references

Three .d.ts declarations (no TypeScript here) and upstream's README, which
PROVENANCE.md replaces. LICENSE stays: MIT requires the notice to travel with
the copy.

Also the three doc lines that still called the deinflector Yomitan's. The
other mentions are about the Yomitan dictionary FORMAT, which is what the app
still reads, and are left alone.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* chore!: relicense MIT, drop the refactor archaeology, unname commercial dicts

BREAKING: the licence changes from GPL-3.0-or-later to MIT.

Nothing copyleft has been in the tree since the deinflector swap, so GPL was
an obligation the code no longer carried — and it is the one that makes App
Store distribution impossible, because Apple's Licensed Application EULA
forbids the redistribution GPLv3 section 10 requires stay unrestricted.
app/package.json stops claiming ISC at the same time; it never was.

docs/history/ goes: 1,143 lines describing restructures that are finished.
Step 4b-3 was NOT finished, and PLAN.md linked into it for the scope, so that
scope now lives in PLAN.md itself — the six files worth typing first, and why
stopping there is the point. Nothing live was in the rest.

Commercial dictionary titles come out of the README and the settings window.
The classifier keeps working, so a zip you own still imports and still labels
itself; the app simply no longer advertises which ones it was built around.

check-conventions.sh globs docs subdirectories instead of history/ by name,
so an empty docs/ does not report its own unexpanded glob as a broken link.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

---------

entry.title: feat: dictionary images, read straight out of the archives (#15)
entry.content:
feat: dictionary images, read straight out of the archives (#15)

Closes #11. The previous PR stopped the broken-image boxes by rendering an
image's label as text; no picture was ever shown. This shows them: Jitendex's
illustrations, 旺文社's stroke-order diagrams, 三省堂's marks.

Nothing is extracted. The issue planned to unpack media at import; measured
first, that is 137 MB across 3,541 files (旺文社 alone 113 MB) on top of a
549 MB index, a second copy to keep in step with the archive, and another
thing to delete on removal. zip.js is lazy — it was made lazy so the settings
list could stop reading 207 MB to learn eight names — so an image request is a
seek and an inflate out of the .zip. The cost is an open archive per
dictionary being read from: bounded at three, dropped whenever the installed
set changes, and measured, because running out of descriptors is what stopped
the app opening a dictionary two commits ago.

Named monochrome marks stay text. 三省堂 draws its 一 二 三 divisions as 128px
glyphs meant to be tinted to the text colour; tinting wants a CSS mask, and a
mask URL is not something this page's policy allows — the first attempt drew
them as solid grey boxes, worse than the text they replaced. Unnamed line art
is drawn and inverted so it is visible on a dark panel, and a full-page
diagram is capped at 130px so it cannot take a tray that is 380px at its
largest.

Images can be turned off (Settings → Lookup). A dictionary is already large
and not every reader wants pictures in a reading popup; with it off an image
becomes the label it carries, which for a sense mark is the whole of its
meaning. Live, like the rest of that tab.

The policy widened by exactly one scheme: img-src yomi-media:. No network, no
file://, no data:. A path out of dictionary data is only ever looked up in
that archive's own directory and never touches a real one, so traversal
cannot happen — media.test.js proves that, that the bytes come back intact,
and that the handles stay bounded across 120 requests.

Verified end to end in a real window with the real preload and the real CSP:
47 images requested, 47 loaded, 0 broken, no policy complaints.

137 node + 11 renderer + 9 settings checks, 0 skipped.

entry.title: feat: dictionaries you can manage, and a popup that reads every one o…
entry.content:
<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>feat: dictionaries you can manage, and a popup that reads every one of them (#14)
* fix: stop the freeze, unite the three dictionary lists, dedupe imports
The freeze had two causes, both synchronous work on the main process.
classify() read a dictionary's whole first bank to look at the second field of its first record. BCCWJ's first bank holds 1,000,219 records — about 100 MB of JSON parsed to read one word — so listing eight archives took 986 ms, on every refresh of the settings window. It now inflates a 64 KB prefix and looks for the tag; 15 ms.
zip.open() read the entire archive to list its names: 207 MB to learn eight of them. It now reads the tail, then exactly the central directory, then an entry's bytes when something asks for them. Rewriting that broke every archive whose tail read covered the whole file — the reconstructed buffer prepended padding and shifted every offset — so the directory is parsed on its own, addressed from its own start.
prune() ran on the main process. Deleting rows is seconds rather than the ~80 a rebuild takes, but seconds of frozen overlay is still frozen, and a progress message cannot be painted by the process busy sending it. It runs in the worker the build already used.
Three lists became one. A dictionary could appear in the priority list and the catalogue at once, and removing it left it behind in the third, still reorderable and answering nothing. Every dictionary is now one row: order on the left, what it is in the middle, the single action that applies on the right.
That bug had a second half in config.js, which merged the saved list with the manifest and never dropped anything: a removed dictionary stayed in the priority list for ever. The saved list is now bounded by what the index actually holds, keeping the user's order and which are switched off. knownDictionaries returns null rather than [] so "no manifest" and "an empty manifest" stay distinguishable.
Importing the same dictionary under a different filename installed it twice — two labels, every sense duplicated. A Yomitan archive names itself in index.json and that is its identity, so an import or download drops any other copy of the same title. Under the same filename it always just overwrote, which was already right.
* test: build the dictionaries the tests need instead of borrowing yours
The dictionary suites read data/dicts/. That directory is gitignored and mostly commercial, so everywhere except this laptop they SKIPPED — CI ran two of the nine node suites and called it green, a fresh clone tested nothing, and keeping copyrighted archives on disk was a precondition for contributing. It also went stale the moment those archives were removed: lookup.test.js failed against an emptied index.db.
A Yomitan archive is an index.json and some bank files in a zip, so the tests now write their own (test/unit/fixtures/make-dictionary.js). That covers more than the real dictionaries did, not less: a deliberately bad CRC, an unknown bank, two archives claiming one title, and all four glossary shapes — where any single real dictionary has one.
The compatibility guarantee needed the old shape, and the honest way to get one is to run the old code: fixtures/legacy-index.js drives build-index.py's own loaders over generated archives, so structured.test.js still compares the renderer against the flattener it replaced, and schema.test.js still proves lookup.js reads both schemas. build-index.py's CREATE TABLE moves into create_schema() so the fixture cannot drift from it.
91 checks, 0 skipped, and they pass in a clone with no data/ at all — so CI now runs all of them rather than two.
Also here, found while writing the coverage:
- Progress read "indexing 100%" the moment an install started. It was reported per ARCHIVE — one dictionary is one step — and the popup drew done + 1. Banks are the unit now, and done counts what has finished. - An emptied index kept every page it had: 448 MB answering nothing. VACUUM after a prune, and delete the file when the last dictionary goes. - Pitch and frequency dictionaries never reached the manifest, so the settings list could not show them or take them out.
* refactor: split the settings window into three files and enforce style with a hook
settings.html was 528 lines: a stylesheet, a program and some markup in one file, which is why it read badly and why its CSP had to allow inline script and style. It is now settings.html / settings.css / settings.js, matching app/renderer, and the page runs under 'self' for both — no 'unsafe-inline' anywhere in the app.
The stylesheet is one declaration per line, sectioned window-top-to-bottom, with the palette as named tokens (seven hex values were repeated across thirty rules). Two dead rules dropped. The declarations were diffed rule-by-rule against the old inline block: identical apart from the four classes replacing inline style attributes.
settings.js gained sections, and lost the things that made it a mess: 1048576 spelled out three times is now inMB(), and the percentage formula that existed in two copies — the copy that caused "indexing 100%" — is one function. The checkbox now leads the row and priority follows it.
Enforcement, so this stops being a matter of who wrote the file:
tools/lint.sh one script, run by tools/hooks/pre-commit AND by CI eslint layout and correctness, config at eslint.config.js swift-format layout, config at .swift-format the compiler Swift types, via ocr/build.sh, already in CI
eslint found more than indentation. renderer.js assigned `lastKey` with no declaration anywhere — an implicit global that worked only because the file is not strict. app/main.js still imported seventeen things it stopped using when it was split up. permissions.js required child_process twice, shadowing itself. glyph-layer.js had its entire body at column zero inside its IIFE.
Adopting swift-format meant reformatting all 25 Swift files at once. Verified byte-identical over the golden corpus first — 66 pages, 5116 glyphs, 132 files, no diff — which is the only reason it is one commit.
New: test/unit/settings.js loads the real page in a hidden Electron window with the real preload, and checks what a fake DOM cannot — that the three files find each other, that the CSP has no unsafe-inline, and that nothing is inline at runtime either. 6 checks. Full suite: 91 node + 11 renderer + 6 settings, 0 skipped.
* fix: the popup lost its typography when it gained the dictionary's structure
Keeping glossary structure instead of flattening it (§8) put the dictionary's own ul/ol/li into the popup, and nothing styled them — so Jitendex went from three lines to half a screen of browser-default bullets. Fixed against Yomitan's own compact glossary layout (its display.css and structured-content.css), and against the real DOM rather than a guess: the first attempt hung its rules off .sc-block, which popup.js never emits, so half of them matched nothing.
· one sense's translations on one line — "origin; beginning; start" · sense numbers in a gutter, with space before the text · example sentences in their own tray, ruby given room, the looked-up word tinted, the English dimmer · part-of-speech as small pills, not list items · no outer bullet beside a structured sense: it brought its own numbering · spelling-variant tables and licence footers hidden, as the old index did (build-index.py's JM_SKIP) — the variants table renders as empty cells, since its markers are images we do not extract yet · body text a point larger
structured.js now carries each node's `data` through as data-sc-* attributes, which is the only thing that says which ul is a list of senses and which is a list of translations; Yomitan does the same. An image we cannot resolve renders its label instead of a broken-image box — 三省堂 ships every sense marker as an SVG.
The dictionary form now heads the card, with the form found on the page under it: 始まる is the word to learn, 始まります is a fact about that sentence.
Two ranking bugs behind the same symptom:
· 神 led with しん (score 0) over かみ (score 200). Entries were sorted by dictionary alone, so the tie fell to rowid order. A term bank's score is its popularity marker; Yomitan sorts on it and now so do we. · frequency chips ignored the priority list, so the arrows beside a frequency dictionary changed nothing at all.
Settings: dictionaries and the trigger now save the moment they change — neither needs the capture child restarted, and lookup.js re-reads the order per lookup. The footer button is therefore only shown on the target-window tab, where it does something, and says what: "Watch this window".
The dictionary list is grouped by state (installed, in priority order / available to download) rather than by provenance. Provenance grouping put a group boundary across one priority list, so an arrow could not move a row past it — which is what made the ordering look broken.
Found by the new test harness: the fake element in dictlist.test.js did not drop children on innerHTML = '', so every "did the rows move" assertion was reading two renders at once.
* fix: lint.sh's own shell bugs, and Swift formatting out of the CI gate
Both found by the first CI run of the check script, which is the point of it.
shellcheck is not installed on this laptop, so tools/lint.sh skipped it here and ran it on the runner — where it flagged the script itself: an unchecked `cd` (SC2164) and an unquoted `$(find)` that would split a path containing a space (SC2046).
swift-format is now hook-only. It ships with Xcode, and the runner's copy breaks lines differently from this machine's: LiveTextEngine.swift:153 is clean locally and two errors there. A gate that fails on which Xcode you have is one nobody can act on. CI still compiles the Swift, which is the type check; formatting is enforced before the commit, where one developer's version is consistent with itself.
* ci: shellcheck must ignore the root node_modules too
The lint tooling brought a node_modules to the repository root, and ajv ships shell scripts with warnings in them. The action was only told to ignore app/node_modules, so the first green lint run failed on a dependency's code.
* fix: queue dictionary work instead of refusing it
"Import a .zip you own…" did nothing while a download or a removal was running. Not disabled — clickable, and silently ignored: the settings window held one global lock and dictAction() returned early.
The lock existed for a real reason. Every one of these jobs writes index.db — a download rebuilds it, a removal prunes it — and two at once race over one file, a rebuild moving index.db.building into place while a prune has the same database open. But a window is the wrong place to enforce that: a second window, or a rebuild the main process starts on its own, sails straight past it.
So the queue lives beside the index, in app/main/job-queue.js. Ask for whatever you like, whenever; it happens in turn. Every progress event now carries the job it belongs to, because with a queue the window can no longer assume that whatever is happening is the thing it last clicked — a row shows its own progress, a row waiting behind another says "waiting…", and only a row with work outstanding is inert.
The queue is its own file rather than a closure inside ipc.js so the tests exercise the queue the app runs. Six checks: no overlap, order preserved, a failure that does not poison the queue behind it, each caller getting its own result, and every event labelled.
104 node + 11 renderer + 8 settings checks, 0 skipped.
* chore: mark the lockfiles as generated
A dependency bump reads as a thousand-line change otherwise. They stay committed, and have to: CI runs `npm ci`, which refuses to run without a lockfile (verified — it exits non-zero), and actions/setup-node keys its cache on one.
* fix: a progress bar that redraws cannot animate, and imports need their own keys
Two things the queue made visible.
The "waiting…" bar never moved. It is drawn as a sliding fill, and a CSS animation restarts from the beginning every time its element is replaced — the whole list was rebuilt on every progress event, and a download reports many times a second, so the row behind it sat frozen at the left edge. The determinate bars had the same problem more quietly: their width transition never got to run either. Progress is now written INTO the bar on screen, and the list is only redrawn when the set of rows changes. Same lesson as the glyph layer (ARCHITECTURE §5): do not rebuild what you can write into.
Importing blocked after the first archive. Every import shared the job key 'import', so a second one looked like the first still running and was refused. Each import now names its own job, and they queue like everything else.
Three checks, in the shape the renderer suite uses — tag the live element and see whether it survived: an update lands in the same bar, a bar that becomes measurable drops its animation, and two imports are two jobs.
* fix: one unreadable archive no longer strands the rest of a multi-select
You asked what happens when three dictionaries are picked at once, so I checked instead of guessing. Three good ones were fine — three copies and ONE index rebuild, which is the point of doing them as a single job.
With a bad one in the middle it was not fine. The loop returned on the first failure, so an archive already copied sat in dicts/ and out of the index: the settings window lists a row per archive, so it showed up installed, offered a Remove button, and answered nothing. Anything after it was never copied at all, and the message named no file.
Every readable archive now goes in, whatever else fails; the ones that could not be read are reported by name ("could not read junk.zip"). The loop moved into dictionaries.importFiles() so the test drives the function the app runs — my first version of this test passed against a copy of the loop written the way it SHOULD work, which is exactly the trap the queue test avoided.
Three checks: three at once, one bad in the middle, and the invariant that makes the list truthful — every archive on disk is one the index knows about.
* fix: the popup styled one dictionary out of eleven
Imported every dictionary — Jitendex, JMnedict, KANJIDIC, JPDB, BCCWJ, 三省堂, 明鏡, 旺文社, 実用, 日本語文法辞典, NHK pitch — rendered 30 diverse entries from each through the real popup, and had five agents read the results: one per dictionary group, one on the combined view, one on the visual system.
They all found the same root cause. The stylesheet was written against Jitendex's node names (`data.content = "sense"`). 三省堂 says `data.name = "語釈"` for the same thing, 明鏡 says `data.meikyo`. So every rule fired for one dictionary and for nothing else: in the monolinguals, examples, cross-references, notes and spelling variants were all styled exactly like definitions, because none of them were styled at all.
structured.js now translates each dictionary's vocabulary into one set of roles (measured from the installed archives, not guessed) and the stylesheet styles roles. That single change is most of what follows:
· examples are quiet indented lines — a tray only when one carries its translation, since a monolingual puts an example under every sense · cross-references dim and small: they point away from this word, and at full weight a Jitendex xref printed a second ① inside an entry · notes, sense numbers, top-level divisions, part-of-speech tags all distinguishable, in every dictionary
Other defects the audits surfaced:
· newlines were dropped in structured entries, so 明鏡's ❶❷❸ ran together as one paragraph — the text carried them, nothing preserved them · 348 empty spans per page from images we cannot draw. A marker's filename names it (一-fill.svg is the division 一); the rest leave nothing behind rather than an empty element · the hanging indent was applied to every line, including prose that starts with no marker, so a wrapped line and a new sense began at the same x · dictKind matched exact labels, so every imported dictionary fell through to a script heuristic — 旺文社 was blue for some entries and green for others, in one card · 下 showed the accents of した, しも, もと and げ all hanging off げ · KANJIDIC's on/kun readings were duplicated into the pitch slot, implying an accent an isolated character does not have · 三省堂's ＊＊ core-vocabulary rank read as stray markdown
And the design pass, from the spec the fifth agent wrote: three tiers by size and brightness rather than by more boxes; headword, reading, pitch and frequency on one sticky line; the deinflection route (始まりました → 始まる ‹-ます·-た›) under it; entries ordered bilingual → monolingual → grammar → kanji → names; reading groups as the divider inside a card, since 神 is かみ and しん and じん; a 2px spine in the dictionary's kind colour instead of a rule between every pair; borderless chips; identical entries deduplicated; proper names demoted to one line at the foot.
118 node + 11 renderer + 8 settings checks, 0 skipped. New: roles.test.js pins the vocabulary mapping, since a dictionary whose names stop being recognised degrades silently to unstyled prose.
* fix: prose dictionaries get the same vocabulary as structured ones
The grammar dictionary answers in plain text, and its structure is in the shape of its lines: [解説] [意味] [例文A] [接続] as headings, a ｜-separated table under the last one, the Japanese and its translation on consecutive lines. None of that was styled, so a 日本語文法辞典 entry was one grey wall while its neighbours had headings, numbered senses and example blocks.
popup.js now reads a plain gloss line by line and classifies each — heading, quotation, table row, numbered sense, 「label：」 prefix — and the stylesheet gives those the SAME treatment as the equivalent roles in structured content. An example looks like an example whichever dictionary it came from, which is the whole point.
Also from that pass:
· 旺文社 wrote 「筆順：」 before a stroke-order diagram we cannot draw, so a colon introduced a two-line hole. A label introducing nothing is dropped. · the ｜ split only handled the full-width form while the detection accepted both, so every ASCII-piped table still showed its pipes · 三省堂's 大語義 WRAPS the senses it divides, so colouring the division turned that dictionary's definitions gold — one dictionary's text a different colour from its neighbours'. The colour goes on the marker. · the pitch downstep was a full-height rule between two characters and read as a text cursor inside the word; it is now a short drop off the end of the overline · Jitendex's footnote markers into a bibliography we do not show are gone
And the hardcoding you asked about. The kanji fallback was gated on the literal label "KANJIDIC", so anyone who imported a different kanji dictionary had it indexed, listed and enabled — and never consulted. It now uses the kanji row's own dict column. dictKind asks the entry's STRUCTURE first (音/訓 readings mean a kanji dictionary whatever it is called) and falls back to the script of the glosses; the names it knows are a shortcut, not the mechanism.
Pitch and frequency were already recognised by what their banks contain rather than by name — kinds.test.js proves it for a pitch pack that is not NHK and a corpus that is neither JPDB nor BCCWJ, and proves that with no pitch dictionary installed nothing claims to know the accent.
That suite immediately caught a regression in this same commit: adding `dict` to the kanji query threw on an index built by the Python builder, which has no such column — and it threw inside open(), failing the whole index rather than its kanji. The column is read only when it is there.
124 node + 11 renderer + 8 settings checks, 0 skipped.
* fix: six findings from reviewing this branch
Two resource leaks, both real and both mine.
classify() opened an archive and handed the handle back in its result, where no caller ever wanted it — so every call leaked a file descriptor. installed() classifies every archive and runs on each settings render, each catalogue() call and after each dictionary job: measured at 133 extra open files after twelve calls with eleven dictionaries. That ends at EMFILE, and a process out of descriptors cannot open a dictionary or spawn the capture helper. The four bank loaders leaked one each for the length of a build. Both now close, and two checks measure it — 60 classifications and a full build must leave nothing open.
Frequency chips would have vanished for every existing user. The new visibility filter treats a source the config has never heard of as hidden, and frequency labels only started reaching the manifest in this same branch — so an upgraded install has JPDB in the index and not in its config, and every chip disappears until something happens to rewrite the manifest. Switched off still means hidden; never heard of now means shown.
Adding the kanji `dict` column to the query broke opening a Python-built index outright: the prepare() throws inside open(), so the whole index fails rather than just its kanji, and every lookup returns null. Read only when the column is there. schema.test.js caught this one on the commit that introduced it.
Two in the line classifier. A bare digit with an optional delimiter matched any line opening with a number, so 「2020年に…」 was given a sense marker's hanging indent; a digit now has to be followed by something that makes it a marker. And a short line ending in a colon was dropped outright to hide 旺文社's 「筆順：」 — which also discarded labels whose content is on the next line. It reads as a heading now: the dangling colon is gone and the meaning is not.
126 node + 11 renderer + 8 settings checks, 0 skipped.
* fix: notice an index that changed underneath, and say when one has not
明鏡 showed up in settings with no checkbox and no priority arrows, looking like it had failed to index. It had indexed fine. The index was rebuilt from outside the app, which changed that dictionary's label, and the running process was still holding the config it read at startup — config.js caches it, and the list of dictionaries in a config is bounded by the manifest, so every dictionary whose label the rebuild changed silently dropped out of it. The window then drew a row from the archives on disk with no config entry behind it, and a row with nothing to enable or order loses its controls.
Two fixes. cfg:get re-reads the manifest before answering, so an index rebuilt by anything other than this process is picked up — a rebuild from the command line, a second window, a restore from backup. And a row whose archive is genuinely not in the index now says so on its own line instead of quietly losing its controls, which was indistinguishable from a bug. It keeps its Remove button, which is the way out.
127 node + 11 renderer + 8 settings checks, 0 skipped.</pre>

entry.title: fix: remove a dictionary in seconds, and say what is happening (#13)
entry.content:
fix: remove a dictionary in seconds, and say what is happening (#13)

* fix: remove a dictionary in seconds, and say what is happening

Four things from using it.

Removing took ~80 seconds because it rebuilt the whole index. The reason
given for that — frequency ordering is global, so everything must be
rebuilt — was wrong. Frequency rows carry the source they came from, so
one dictionary's removal cannot disturb another's ranking and nothing is
recomputed across dictionaries. Removal now deletes that dictionary's
rows: measured 930ms for the terms and 1,665ms for the glossaries left
with nothing pointing at them, against ~80,000ms.

Two things had to change for that to be possible. kanji and pitch had no
column saying which dictionary a row came from, so those rows could not
be found again; every table has one now. And the orphan sweep is an
anti-join that took 4,192ms unindexed, so idx_terms_gloss exists — 580ms
to build, once.

test/unit/prune.test.js asserts the equivalence the whole thing rests on:
an index with a dictionary pruned out holds exactly what an index built
without that dictionary holds, compared table by table, including the
frequency source that has to survive. An index built before the dict
columns existed cannot be pruned, reports that, and is rebuilt instead.

Removal had no feedback at all. It now reports its phase, and indexing
reports a percentage rather than a bare word.

An expanded app in the window list could never be collapsed — the click
handler only ever added to the expanded set. It toggles, and the hint
says which way the next click goes.

Remove sits at the left of the row it acts on, where the eye starts,
rather than drifting away from long dictionary titles.

* test: check what the removal change could have broken

Four specific ways the schema change could have gone wrong, each checked
rather than assumed: an index built before the dict columns must refuse
to be pruned and keep every table intact; the manifest derived from the
database must match the order build() loaded dictionaries in, or removing
one silently reorders the popup; pitch rows must still load after the
insert gained a column; and lookup must still answer against an index
carrying the new columns.

entry.title: feat: import dictionaries in the app, and ship without one (#10)
entry.content:
feat: import dictionaries in the app, and ship without one (#10)

* feat: read dictionary archives and keep their glossary structure

Groundwork for importing a dictionary from the Settings window, which is
how someone uses a commercial monolingual the app can never ship.

app/main/zip.js reads Yomitan archives with nothing but node:zlib — the
central directory is a fixed layout and DEFLATE is in the stdlib, so the
alternative was Yomitan's zip.js as this app's first runtime dependency.
Verified against all twelve archives here, including the NHK pitch pack,
whose CRCs do not match its contents; the Python builder carries the same
tolerance for the same reason.

app/main/index-builder.js stores each glossary's STRUCTURE rather than
flattening it to sense strings at index time. Flattening only works for
formats someone taught the builder and degrades to a permissive walk for
everything else — the walk that yields 「き」「ぞく」「［」 as three senses.
Since the point is a dictionary nobody anticipated, the structure is kept
and rendered at display time, as Yomitan does.

Verbatim structure cost 1,670 MB against the old index's 322 MB, so
glossaries are deduplicated into their own table and deflated: measured
1,068 MB of glossary across 2,005,802 rows of which only 463 MB was
distinct, and structured JSON deflates to ~35%. That lands at 510 MB —
188 MB more than flattening, for a dictionary format nobody has to
anticipate. Both halves are asserted lossless.

lookup.js reads either shape, decided once at open() by whether a glosses
table exists. An index built by the old Python builder is still a good
dictionary and must keep answering across an update. open() takes a path
so that claim is testable, and close() lets a freshly imported index be
picked up without a restart.

Checks: test/unit/index-builder.test.js asserts glossaries round-trip
byte-identical through dedupe and compression, that every usable record
is indexed under every key it names, that kanji counts match the archive,
that no term points at a missing glossary, and that a non-dictionary zip
is reported rather than indexed. test/unit/schema.test.js opens a real
old index and a freshly built new one and requires the same answer.

* feat: render structured content, checked against what it replaces

app/renderer/structured.js turns a stored glossary into DOM. Written
against a census of what the twelve dictionaries here actually contain —
14 tags, 7 style properties, two node types — rather than against the
format in the abstract. Yomitan's own generator is ~550 lines because it
also carries their media pipeline, Anki rendering and language detection,
and its contentManager interface would have to be stubbed to something
this app has no use for.

An unrecognised tag is not dropped: it becomes a neutral inline or block
element and its children still render. A dictionary nobody has seen is
the entire reason the structure is kept.

The old index-time flattener is the oracle. It was written with real
per-dictionary knowledge, so whatever text it displayed the renderer must
still display; test/unit/structured.test.js asserts that over a fixed
slice of 3,000 keys in key order — 7,918 senses across all eight
dictionaries, none lost.

Getting that check honest took four corrections, each a real finding:

- textOf dropped images. 三省堂 sets sense markers (ⓑ) and part-of-speech
  tags as SVG logos with the character in title, so an image that carries
  a label is text to a reader.
- Substring was the wrong relation. The new rendering carries MORE: the
  old flattener dropped the bracketed headword 三省堂 prints between a
  sense number and its text, storing 「① 円の形」 where the dictionary
  reads 「①［円］円の形」. Subsequence, ordered.
- Markers are not words. The old builder synthesised its own numbering
  and read sense numbers out of listStyleType to inline them; the
  renderer sets that as CSS and lets the browser draw the marker.
- The checker itself was wrong outside the BMP: it walked the haystack by
  code point and the needle by UTF-16 code unit, so 明鏡's 𠤎 (U+2090E)
  in あいくち could never match.

* feat: add and remove dictionaries from the settings window

Downloads the freely licensed ones by name and imports the ones a user
owns, which is the only way 三省堂 or DOJG can ever reach the app — they
cannot ship with it and cannot be offered for download.

The catalogue mirrors what Yomitan itself recommends, checked against
yomitan.wiki/dictionaries rather than assumed: Jitendex from
stephenmk/stephenmk.github.io (the stephenmk/Jitendex path now redirects),
JMnedict and KANJIDIC from the jmdict-yomitan daily builds, both
frequency lists from Kuuuube. All five resolve live and were verified to
return 200 with plausible sizes.

Nothing is pinned by filename. The GitHub entries resolve the latest
release when asked; the Kuuuube ones match a pattern against the repo
tree and take the newest, because that repository keeps old versions
beside new — JPDB v2.1 is still sitting next to v2.2, so a pinned name
would have quietly fetched a stale build forever.

The rebuild runs in a forked worker. node:sqlite is synchronous and a
full rebuild is ~80 seconds; in the main process that freezes the tray,
the settings window and the overlay panel, which is drawn over whatever
the user is reading. ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE, so it is the same binary.

popup.js renders whatever a dictionary wrote. Plain strings keep the
formatting they had; structured content is built as DOM by structured.js
and stubbed into the markup, since it cannot be expressed as a string.
Without this an import would have replaced a working index with a
structured one and every sense would have rendered as [object Object].

config.js reads the manifest from wherever the index actually is — the
user's own wins, matching lookup.js — and can be told to forget its cache,
so a dictionary imported now appears in the list without a restart.

Downloads land on a .part file and are validated as a real Yomitan
archive before being named, so a 404 page cannot install itself as a
dictionary. remove() takes a basename, so a crafted name cannot reach out
of the dictionaries folder.

* feat: ship no dictionary, and let the app fetch or import one

The release bundle carried a 189 MB index built from the freely licensed
set. Now it carries none: measured 465 MB -> 276 MB, of which Electron is
nearly all of what remains.

This also removes the licensing question from the release rather than
policing it. build-release.sh used to refuse to package an index whose
manifest named a commercial dictionary, and release.yml built the index
on a clean runner so it was free by construction. Neither is needed when
nothing licensed is in the bundle at all — a stronger position than
checking.

A fresh install therefore has no dictionary, which is now a normal state
rather than an error. main.js opens the settings window and says where to
get one instead of naming a Python script the user does not have.
config.js no longer falls back to the built-in list of nine names when no
manifest exists, because showing a new install dictionaries it does not
have is worse than showing none; an install predating the manifest is
unaffected, since its own config.json already carries the list.

Capture, OCR and the glyph layer all work before a dictionary exists.
Only lookups have nothing to answer with.

ARCHITECTURE section 8 said structure is extracted at index time and
explained why, with the 「き」「ぞく」「［」 measurement that paid for it.
That decision is reversed and the section now says what replaced it and
what it cost: 1,670 MB verbatim, 510 MB after deduplicating and
deflating, against 322 MB flattened. Section 13 documents where
dictionaries come from, why a rebuild is total and why it runs in a
forked worker. Section 6 no longer promises a bundled index.

Images are deferred and said so: 10,732 img nodes across these
dictionaries, only 35% carrying a usable title, and a renderer CSP of
default-src 'none'. They render as alt text until media extraction and a
narrow protocol exist.

Verified by building the bundle: 276 MB, and a find for *.db and
dictionaries.json inside it returns nothing.

entry.title: feat: a downloadable app, released and versioned automatically (#8)
entry.content:
feat: a downloadable app, released and versioned automatically (#8)

* feat: a downloadable app, and the release pipeline that builds it

`tools/build-release.sh` produces a bundle that runs on a machine with no
checkout, no Xcode and no dictionary download, and release.yml builds it
on a tag once CI passes.

The bundling is one extra candidate. bootstrap.js already probed
$YOMI_OVERLAY_DIR, then a pointer file, then a hardcoded fallback;
Contents/Resources is now tried LAST, so a developer's pointer file still
wins and "restart, don't rebuild" is untouched (ARCHITECTURE §6).
paths.js notices which happened and splits what was one `data/` into the
two ideas it always was: read-only material inside the signed bundle
(index, manifest, yomi) and what the user writes (config, an index of
their own). In a checkout both resolve to `data/`, so development is
byte-for-byte unchanged.

lookup.js prefers a user index over the bundled one, so anyone can build
index.db over their own dictionaries and drop it beside their config
without touching a signed bundle.

Licensing is why the release is built in CI rather than on a laptop. A
runner starts clean, so fetch-dicts.py — which only knows how to download
freely-licensed sources — is the only thing that puts a dictionary on
disk. build-release.sh re-checks that before packaging, against both the
zips present AND what dictionaries.json says is in the index, because a
stale index outlives the zips it came from. Run here today it refuses,
naming 三省堂, 明鏡, 旺文社, 実用, DOJG, どんなとき and NHK pitch.

Signing is a drop-in: a Developer ID is used when the secrets exist and
ad-hoc otherwise. Ad-hoc means the download is quarantined and the TCC
identity changes per build, which the release notes say plainly.

Verified end to end: a free index (189 MB, Jitendex + JMnedict +
KANJIDIC) built from a clean tree, packaged to a 465 MB bundle, launched
with no checkout in scope — the dictionary opened from Resources and the
trigger came back as the default rather than this machine's configured
one, which is what proves config resolved to Application Support.

* feat: work the release version out from the commits, and tag in the pipeline

* docs: RELEASING.md — how a PR title becomes a version

Squash-merge means the PR title IS the commit subject the release
pipeline parses, which is the one thing an author needs to know and the
one thing nothing currently said. Tabulates what to write for each
digit, why an unrecognised prefix bumps the patch rather than being
ignored, why 1.0.0 stays manual, and why there is no digit rollover.

Indexed in docs/README.md and pointed at from CONVENTIONS' workflow
section.

entry.title: perf: cut a changed watch pass from ~1.8s to ~0.85s (#6)
entry.content:
perf: cut a changed watch pass from ~1.8s to ~0.85s (#6)

Four changes to the capture loop, each measured before and after. No
recognised output moved: the golden corpus is byte-identical across all
66 images, and CER over 106 ground-truth crops is unchanged at 0.0115.

- One window enumeration per pass, not two. SCShareableContent costs
  ~150ms and was paid by both chooseWindow and captureOnce. Cached and
  invalidated by the compositing window set (CGWindowList, 0.5ms), never
  by a timer alone — a window that appeared between refreshes would be
  captured. Frames now come from CGWindowList every pass, since the
  cached SCWindow's own frame goes stale.

- The Live Text mixed-content merge runs only when Vision left a mark
  unaccounted for. It cost 1.35s against the 0.85s read it supplements,
  on every changed pass, whether or not there was anything to merge.
  38 committed-horizontal ground-truth pages: identical text on all 38,
  skipped on 34, 0.69s -> 0.35s. On a full clean page, 1.8s -> 0.85s.
  Needed a polarity-independent mask — inkMask read a dark-mode page as
  100% ink, which would have defeated the gate for anyone reading dark.

- A pass that emitted new text waits 0.1s, not the interval: the frame
  it read was captured a whole pass ago. Bounded at three in a row so an
  animated page cannot pin the recogniser.

- buildPayload writes one string instead of a String per glyph joined
  per line; jsonEscape stops allocating for text that needs no escaping.

Session.noteOnce replaces the two "print only when this changes" fields
the diagnostics had each grown, and the write half of logEngineOnce.

Measured over a real reading session: page-turn cycle p50 3.62s -> 2.57s,
recognition p50 2.18s -> 1.61s.
