entry.title: Restructure: split the monolith, add unattended tests, harden IPC (#1)
entry.content:
<pre style='white-space:pre-wrap;width:81ex'>Restructure: split the monolith, add unattended tests, harden IPC (#1)
* docs: refactoring diagnosis and executable integration plan
REFACTOR.md is the diagnosis: per-file concern counts, the missing abstractions, and why the folder layout is shaped the way it is (paths.js deliberately conflates code and data location, which is what makes the restart-don't-rebuild property in ARCHITECTURE section 6 work).
REFACTOR-INTEGRATION.md is the procedure: ordered steps, each with an explicit gate, plus the sourced findings that changed the plan — Electron's main/preload/renderer convention, sandbox already being on by default since Electron 20, package-by-feature's single-delete modularity test, the Swift rule of threes, and phantom types as the standard idiom for coordinate spaces.
* test: golden-master harness for the refactor
Structural changes must not move a byte of kindleocr's output. This makes that checkable instead of aspirational.
--image is the right harness and already existed: it opens no ScreenCaptureKit session and needs no Screen Recording grant, so it runs headlessly and, verified here, while the overlay is running — a one-shot --dump capture would stall on the concurrent SCK session.
Both stdout and stderr are recorded. The engine/orientation/furigana diagnostics are the only visible signal for policy decisions that leave the payload unchanged, so a stdout-only diff would pass an orientation probe that silently started committing horizontal.
The corpus is a fixed 66-image list, not a find(1) walk: test/gt holds ~3800 rendered pages. Every image from the hand-built categories plus every 100th epub page covers both orientations, furigana, mixed content and the native vertical path in 37s. Measured: 197 lines, 5116 glyphs, zero empty payloads, 33 of 66 vertical-flagged.
Determinism was verified, not assumed — Vision is nondeterministic between captures, but two full passes over fixed PNGs came back byte identical.
The glyph floor exists because a harness that passes when nothing was recognised is a broken harness. check already catches total failure (an all-empty run cannot match a populated baseline), but record would freeze a broken baseline in and every later check would compare two identical piles of nothing.
* refactor: one path resolver per language, layout unchanged
Seven places independently knew the directory layout: paths.js, bootstrap.js, build-app.sh, setup.sh, build-index.py, fetch-dicts.py, main.js (the .venv path) and six test files (REPO/kindleocr). Any folder change had to be made correctly in all of them at once.
paths.js was one constant, DATA_DIR, doing the work of seven ideas that happen to share a directory today — the app code, the renderer, the settings window, the preloads, the tray assets, the generated data, and the Python venv. That conflation is deliberate and load-bearing (ARCHITECTURE section 6: the bundle holds only a loader, so code and data resolve to the same place), but it means the layout cannot move without touching every consumer. Splitting the roots keeps the property and removes the coupling.
paths.py and paths.sh give the Python and shell scripts the same service, each deriving every root from its own location. No literal path survives anywhere except one line per resolver, marked as the only line that knows the layout.
Every root still resolves exactly where it did before: this commit moves no file and changes no behaviour. Verified byte-identical against the golden-master baseline (66 payloads, 5116 glyphs), every resolved path exists, and all JS/Python parses.
Dead pathlib imports dropped from the two Python scripts that no longer construct paths themselves.
* refactor: domain folder structure
Pure move plus the layout lines in the three resolvers. No logic changed; git records every file as a rename, so history follows.
overlay/ held five unrelated things at one level — main-process code, the renderer, the settings window, the dictionary build pipeline, a Python ML sidecar, app packaging, and ~470 MB of generated data. Now:
ocr/Sources the Swift helper (build with ocr/build.sh) app/ main.js + main/ renderer/ settings/ preload/ assets/ shell/ vendor/ tools/ build and side scripts, bundle inputs, the resolvers data/ generated + licensed: index.db, dicts/, config.json, .venv bin/ compiled helpers docs/ ARCHITECTURE CONVENTIONS PLAN INTEGRATION REFACTOR*
preload/ is top-level rather than beside the code it isolates because those two files are the entire trust boundary between the renderer and Node, and because Electron treats preload as a third process context with its own rules. Burying them next to what they expose is what made that boundary easy to overlook.
icon.icns and extend.plist went to tools/, NOT app/shell/, despite being bundle inputs: electron-packager copies the shell directory wholesale into the .app, so anything parked there gets baked into the bundle. app/shell/ still contains only the loader — that is ARCHITECTURE section 6, and it is what keeps the bundle hash stable and the TCC grants alive.
.gitignore collapses from six artifact rules to data/ + bin/ + app/node_modules/: what is generated is now a property of the layout instead of a list that has to be kept in sync. overlay/dicts/.gitkeep went with it — data/ is wholly ignored and fetch-dicts.py creates the directory itself.
ocr/build.sh replaces the inline swiftc line, and globs Sources/ so the step-4 file split needs no build change.
Verified: golden-master byte identical with the moved binary AND again after a full rebuild through the new build script (66 payloads, 5116 glyphs); all eleven roots and every file resolved through them exist; every JS, Python and shell file parses; no doc link is broken.
* refactor: split KindleOCR.swift into files by pipeline stage
Mechanical extraction only. No renames, no signature changes, no logic edits. The one deliberate exception is access level: splitting a file breaks `private` at file scope, so inkMask and runs — used by BOTH Tategaki and Furigana — widen to internal. shoot keeps private; its only caller moved with it.
2756 lines -> 18 files, largest now 485:
Capture/ WindowSelection Capture CropChannel Recognition/ Orientation LiveTextEngine VisionEngine Recognizer Voting Geometry/ Spaces Ink Tategaki Furigana Model/ Line Output/ Payload Diagnostics CLI/ Options EventsCommand Entry.swift
Grouped by pipeline stage rather than by type, because Capture, Recognition, Tategaki and Furigana are problem-domain words here — the folder names should name what this tool does, not what kind of construct each file holds. A Models/Services/Utils split would have said nothing.
Done as a verified partition rather than by eye: the 2757 lines were cut into 65 contiguous blocks with no gaps or overlaps, each block assigned to exactly one file, and every non-blank source line then compared as a multiset against the original. The only two lines that differ are the two private declarations widened above.
ocr/build.sh now discovers sources recursively. A read loop, not mapfile — macOS ships bash 3.2 — and sorted, so the compiler sees a stable order.
Verified: compiles clean with no warnings, and golden-master byte identical (66 payloads, 5116 glyphs, 132 files).
* docs: record two findings from the refactor, unfixed
Both are behaviour changes, so neither belongs in a structural commit.
1. The capture-recovery notice is unreachable in JSON watch mode — it sits after the branch that continues, so the only path the overlay uses never prints it and never resets the failure counter. Cost: you cannot tell 'failed once and recovered' from 'still failing'. Hit this while diagnosing a -3811 today and had to answer it with --list-all instead.
2. setup.sh says rebuilding kindleocr costs nothing. Measured: it costs the first capture after the rebuild, which is refused with -3801 before the supervisor restarts the child and everything works. The grant does survive; the docs are what is wrong. Which of the cdhash or the path change triggers it is still open — both moved at once, and the note records the experiment that would separate them.
* refactor: split Main.main() into one file per subcommand
Finishes the mechanical phase. Main.main() was 451 lines with all six subcommands inlined; it is now 52 lines of dispatch and nothing else.
CLI/PermissionCommand --check-permission CLI/ImageCommand --image CLI/EventsCommand --events (joins the monitor it starts) CLI/ListCommand --list-all, --debug, --list, --frame CLI/WatchCommand --watch, plus waitNextPass, its only caller
Bodies moved verbatim. The one unavoidable edit is indentation: every branch was over-indented by twelve spaces — the fossil of a switch that had been removed — and a body extracted into a top-level function has to sit at four. Dedent is uniform per block, which is what keeps the multi-line string literals in --list-all and --frame intact: Swift strips indentation relative to the closing delimiter, and the delimiter moves with the content.
Ranges came from brace matching rather than reading, which caught one branch I had miscounted by six lines.
Verified: compiles clean; golden-master byte identical. Golden only drives --image, though, so the four CLI paths it cannot see were checked by hand: --check-permission returns its JSON, --list-all parses with all nine keys, --list prints the target window, --frame emits valid JSON. The last two are where the dedented string literals live, so that was the check that mattered.
* refactor: per-run recognition state becomes RecognitionSession
Six file-scope vars — orientation, engineMode, debugDumpPath, flatReadNativeVertical, lastMixedNote, lastLoggedEngine — were never global facts. Each is what ONE run has learned: which way this page reads, whether the last flat read came back native-vertical, which diagnostics have already been printed.
Keeping them global had a concrete cost. Nothing could set up a starting state, which is why --assume-horizontal exists as a production CLI flag: it is a constructor argument wearing a command-line flag's clothes, and its own comment says so ('a one-shot --image run always starts at .unknown, so the committed-horizontal code paths are otherwise untestable headlessly'). It is now RecognitionSession(orientation: .horizontal), with the flag kept as the public spelling of it.
A class, not a struct: recognizeAuto commits the orientation it discovers and recognize() reports back what shape the flat read had, and both must be visible to the caller afterwards.
Two related fixes fall out. engineMode was a global that parseArgs wrote as a side effect — it is now Options.engine, a parsed option like every other, and the same for debugDumpPath. And buildPayload read lastLoggedEngine straight out of the air to fill the payload's engine field; it now takes it as an argument, so the serializer no longer reaches into recognition state.
The watch loop builds ONE session and keeps it, because orientation being sticky across passes is the point of caching it; --image builds one per run.
Verified: golden-master byte identical (the engine field is in every payload, so this covers the threading). Golden cannot see the session-only flags, so those were checked by hand: --assume-horizontal skips the probe and takes the committed path with the furigana strip active, --engine vision forces Vision, and the default still probes livetext then vision before committing.
Remaining file-scope state is capture-side (target, lastOccluders) and is a WindowTracker, not this change.
* refactor: give the shared recognition shape a home of its own
Vision and Live Text are both normalized to one intermediate shape — lines with per-character boxes in top-left normalized subject coordinates — so that everything downstream never learns which engine ran. That shape lived inside LiveText, which meant the Vision path returned [LiveText.RLine]: the Vision function's return type was named after the other engine. Nothing was broken; the name was admitting the shared currency had no home.
It has one now: RecognizedLine / RecognizedChar in Recognition/Engine.swift.
Deliberately NOT the RecognitionEngine protocol the plan called for. Reading the call sites changed the answer:
- LiveText.analyze is async and returns nil for "failed this pass, fall back"; visionLines throws and takes unrotate and wantChars, which have no Live Text analogue. A common signature means dead parameters on one side. - verticalRemainder calls Live Text by name on purpose. Vision reads no vertical Japanese at all, so there is no engine-agnostic version of it. - Choosing between them is a policy paid for in measurements (0.3% vs 0.6% CER horizontal, 89% vs 66% placement on the reflow strip). A protocol would sit above that if/else without removing it, and the if/else is the product.
One shared vocabulary, two named engines, an explicit policy — and the reasoning recorded in Engine.swift so it is not re-litigated.
Verified: golden-master byte identical. The only LiveText references left outside its own file are the two intentional ones, plus the note explaining why they are intentional.
* refactor: break recognize() into orchestration plus four named steps
recognize() was 343 lines doing seven jobs. It is now 118 — of which about 75 are the engine-policy comment block, which stays exactly where it is because it explains the dispatch it sits above.
Extracted, bodies unchanged:
stripFurigana -> Geometry/Furigana.swift, joining the ruby code it belongs to. Returns the cleaned image and the hints, instead of mutating two variables in an enclosing scope. mapReflowedStrip -> Recognition/Mapping.swift mapFlatLines -> Recognition/Mapping.swift attachHints -> Recognition/Mapping.swift
Three mappers in one file, which is what earns it: each takes recognised boxes and puts them back on the page, and each was previously an anonymous block in the middle of a function doing something else.
mapFlatLines takes fromLiveText where the block read `raw != nil` — same value, but a parameter has to say what it means, and what it means is "this read came from Live Text, so judge each line's orientation on its own char quads".
Two slicing mistakes on the first attempt, both caught by the compiler rather than by review: stripEligible got declared twice, and the 16-line engine policy comment was dropped. Redone from brace-matched boundaries.
Verified: golden-master byte identical.
* docs: scope the phantom-typed rects and defer them
Measured rather than estimated: 72 CGRect/CGPoint/CGSize sites across 16 of the 24 Swift files, spanning five coordinate spaces. A rect type worth having has to carry the whole surface the code uses, and half-applied it is worse than CGRect — some sites converting, some not, no guarantee anywhere. That makes it its own piece of work, not the tail of this one.
The note records the hazard it would fix, which is live: RecognizedLine.box is normalised top-left, Line.box is normalised bottom-left, both are bare CGRect, and mapFlatLines converts between them inside one expression. Three comments warn about it; nothing enforces it.
Also records the recommended first slice — type only the normalised pair and make NBox the sole conversion, six files rather than sixteen — and the fact that golden-master covers every one of those conversions, so a sign error fails loudly rather than silently misplacing glyphs.
* refactor: rename the capture helper from kindleocr to yomi
The name was a misnomer and contradicted the project's own principle. The overlay works over any macOS window — browsers, manga readers, PDF viewers, fullscreen games — and CONVENTIONS.md says in as many words: "No per-app special cases. A fix that keys on a bundle id is the wrong fix." The helper was named after one of its many targets.
yomi (読み, "reading") says what it does without naming a vendor, and matches the app it serves.
111 occurrences across 24 files: the binary, the path resolvers in all three languages, the four test suites, the golden harness, and every doc. The KINDLEOCR variable in main.js, golden.sh, cer.py and cellbench.py becomes YOMI_BIN rather than bare YOMI, so it still reads as a path.
Kept deliberately:
- defaultBundleIDs and the config default target. Kindle is still the default target; it just is not the only one, which is the whole point. - KindleOCR.swift where the historical docs name the pre-split file. That file existed and the record should say so. - The FOUND-BUGS note's paths, which record what they actually were at the time — the sweep had rewritten that history and it is restored.
Verified: golden-master byte identical (the baseline contains no occurrence of either name, checked before renaming, so this was a real gate rather than a tautology), and the four CLI paths golden cannot see still work.
* refactor: stop calling the target window "Kindle"
Twenty comments and six user-facing strings described the thing being captured as "Kindle" — the overlay pinned to "the Kindle window", focus staying "with Kindle", clicks falling "through to Kindle", a capture timeout blaming "Kindle in native fullscreen". None of that is true. The overlay works over browsers, manga readers, PDF viewers and fullscreen games, and CONVENTIONS.md is explicit that keying on one app is the wrong shape.
Reworded to "the target", including the strings a user actually sees: the --frame help line, the --list "no matching windows found", the capture-timeout error, the idle-hide log line, and the renderer's window title.
Left alone on purpose:
- Every measurement that was taken ON a Kindle page — the ruby fusion (別天神+ことあまつかみ -> 前実), the per-slice projection finding zero bands, the +1-char span shift on ruby-spread text, the 618-vs-6 vertical read, the zoom-while-pinned popup bug. Those record where the number came from, and CONVENTIONS says not to remove them. - The default target and its bundle ids. Kindle is still the default; it is just not the only one. - README and settings.html listing Kindle as an example target, which is what it is.
Two things this surfaced, both left for their own commits because they are behaviour, not wording: the settings picker's skip-list names a bundle id (local.kindleoverlay) that the app has not used since it was renamed to local.yomioverlay, and --debug still filters candidate windows on the literal string "kindle" — a per-app special case in exactly the place CONVENTIONS warns about.
Verified: golden-master byte identical; no test parses any reworded string.
* fix: settings picker was skipping a bundle id the app no longer has
The window picker's skip-list named local.kindleoverlay. The app's bundle id is local.yomioverlay — build-app.sh sets it and setup.sh resets TCC against it — so the list filtered a nonexistent app and let the real one through.
Effect: the overlay's own settings window (560x520, past the 400x300 floor) appeared in its own target picker, offering the user the chance to point the overlay at itself.
Found by the rename sweep, and kept out of it: renaming a string is structural, correcting which window gets filtered is behaviour.
* test: unattended suites for lookup and the renderer
Twenty tests that need no permission, no visible window and no network, so steps 5 and 6 stop depending on hands-on checking.
lookup.test.js (9) runs in plain node against the real index.db. This code had no test at all despite being the hot path behind every popup: it covers deinflection (見つけた -> 見つける), multi-length grouping and the ranking order, glyph-counted matchLength, the single-kanji fallback with 音/訓 kept apart, NFKC normalisation of OCR codepoint twins, and the empty-input and maxLen edges. Assertions are about shape and order, not gloss wording — the dictionaries are user-supplied and their text is not ours to pin.
renderer.js (11) drives app/renderer/index.html as a black box in a HIDDEN Electron window, through the real preload and the real IPC channel names, with payloads captured from the ground-truth corpus. It covers the rebuild gate from ARCHITECTURE section 5, which is the subtlest logic in the project and had no coverage: identical payload, a >85% similar payload refused, the bounded-refusal escape after three, a page turn, a pure re-layout, and a voted payload patched in place rather than rebuilt — plus placement, reset, dismiss, and a lookup refused inside a cover region.
Two things make it honest. It uses the REAL preload and the real isolation settings, so it exercises the same trust boundary the app does. And rebuilds are observable from outside because a rebuild does layer.innerHTML = '': a property set on a live span survives if and only if the layer was not rebuilt.
That last point is why this exists NOW rather than after step 6. The renderer logic is inline in index.html and cannot be imported, so tests written after the extraction could not have guarded the extraction. Recorded first, same discipline as golden.sh.
The first fixture had 2 lines, so changing one line put similarity at 50% and the layer correctly rebuilt — the test was wrong, not the code. Replaced with a 19-line payload from the corpus, where one changed line sits at 94.7%.
Also fixes a stale ../overlay/node_modules path in test/README.md left over from the step-3 move.
* test: characterize child supervision, and extract it into SupervisedChild
Written before the step-5 split rather than after, so the extraction is guarded by what main.js already did rather than by what the new code happens to do. Fifteen assertions, each naming the behaviour it pins:
- NDJSON parsed per LINE, carrying a partial line across chunk boundaries. A payload with two thousand glyph boxes is several kilobytes, so `{"frame":{"x":0` is an ordinary read, not a hypothetical one. - blank and unparseable lines skipped, not fatal - an unexpected exit restarts; the backoff doubles and is capped; a healthy result resets it - stop() does NOT restart — the `deliberate` flag - a STALE process exiting cannot schedule a restart over the live one - a child that ignores SIGTERM is escalated to SIGKILL - silence while still running trips the watchdog; a talking child does not - a missing binary is reported, not thrown - write() reaches the child's stdin and is safe when there is none
app/main/ndjson.js and app/main/supervised-child.js are added but not yet wired in; the next commit replaces the duplicated copies with them. The splitter existed three times (capture child, event monitor, tier-2 sidecar) and the restart logic twice, with the state spread across six module-scope variables plus a flag stapled onto the ChildProcess object.
The stub child needs no binary, no permission and no window, so this runs unattended alongside the other suites.
* refactor: both helper children become SupervisedChild instances
startOCR and startEvents were near-identical: spawn, report a spawn failure, buffer NDJSON off stdout, restart on an unexpected exit with a backoff, skip the restart when we killed it deliberately. The NDJSON splitter was written out three times and the restart logic twice, with the state spread across six module-scope variables plus a `deliberate` flag stapled onto the ChildProcess.
Now two constructions and two callbacks. main.js keeps only what is actually app-specific: onOcrLine, which routes payload / heartbeat / idle / crop and is the whole overlay in one function, and onTriggerEvent, which rebases a global click into window coordinates.
The two children differ in exactly the two ways that were always real, and they are now stated rather than duplicated: the capture child escalates its backoff 1s→30s and carries a 120s silence watchdog; the event monitor uses a flat 2s and has none, because it either has Accessibility or it does not and there is nothing for a growing backoff to wait out.
The watchdog moves inside the class, so the 30s setInterval and the four variables it read (ocr, ocrRestartTimer, ocrLastOutput, ocrWatchdogFired) are gone. stopChild is gone. Restart-on-retarget, the tray's Restart capture, and the modifier-change restart are all one call now.
exitHint keeps the capture child's exit diagnostic pointing at its own stderr — that line has earned its keep and CONVENTIONS says so.
Verified: 24 node assertions plus 11 renderer assertions green, and the child suite is the characterization written BEFORE this change. Still unverified by a launch — no automated coverage reaches the panel, the tray or the sidecar yet, so this needs a hands-on run before step 5 continues.
* refactor: take the stylesheet and renderer script out of index.html
index.html was 739 lines: 134 of CSS, 12 of markup, and a 583-line inline script. It is now 22 lines that say what the page is made of.
Nothing moved but whitespace — the CSS and the script are byte-for-byte what they were, in overlay.css and renderer.js. Splitting renderer.js into its actual pieces is the next commit; doing both at once would have made the diff unreadable and the failure ambiguous.
With nothing inline left, the CSP drops 'unsafe-inline' from BOTH script-src and style-src. The renderer can now only run code that shipped with it. That was on the PLAN.md Stage 6 list as security hardening; it turned out to be a consequence of the split rather than a task of its own.
Verified: all 11 renderer assertions green. They drive this page as a black box through the real preload, so they cover the move end to end.
* refactor: split the renderer into layer, placement, hud and coordinator
renderer.js was 583 lines holding six jobs. Now:
glyph-layer.js the span layer and its rebuild gate placement.js where that layer sits, and what is drawn over it hud.js the transient status line renderer.js the decisions between them popup.js unchanged — it was already the right shape
glyph-layer.js is the point of the exercise. One invariant used to be spread across eight module-scope variables and three hundred lines: contentSig must always describe what is actually in the DOM. Advancing it while keeping old spans is what let drift ratchet (ARCHITECTURE section 5). It now has a file to itself and a stated contract.
apply() returns one of four named outcomes — identical / patched / kept / rebuilt — which were previously four unlabelled exits from one 149-line function. The caller uses that name instead of inferring: 'rebuilt' is what invalidates the lookup key and refreshes the HUD.
Deliberately an IIFE exposing a window namespace, not a class. That is the pattern popup.js already established, and more importantly it needed NO renaming inside the moved code — the risky part travels verbatim, and only the exits and the two lines that reached outside changed.
Verified: all 11 renderer assertions green, unchanged. They were recorded against the pre-split index.html precisely so they could not be tuned to the new shape.
* refactor: extract logging, tier-2, the window list and the settings window
main.js 740 -> 542 lines, module-scope variables 17 -> 9.
log.js the file-mirroring logger and the console hooks tier2.js the manga-ocr sidecar window-list.js the picker's candidate filtering settings-window.js the app's only ordinary window
tier2 is the one worth naming. Nine module-scope variables, a pending map and a queue sat at the top of main.js for a single optional feature that is off by default. They are one session, so they are one factory now, and main.js asks it for exactly one thing: onCropReply.
It takes ocrChild as a parameter rather than reaching for it, which states the real dependency — the crop is served by the watch process cropping its own last frame, because a second ScreenCaptureKit session would stall.
Verified three ways: all 35 assertions green; and a load-time smoke test that actually ran main.js under Electron for five seconds, reaching "app ready", building the tray, spawning both children, loading the deinflector and pushing trigger config to the renderer, with no reference errors. That is the check node --check cannot make, and it caught nothing only because two earlier slicing mistakes had already been fixed.
* refactor: the panel becomes overlay-window.js
main.js 542 -> 340 lines, module-scope variables 9 -> 4.
Five variables described one window: win, interactive, idleTimer, and the last offset and cover signature sent to the renderer. Both of those last two exist only to avoid resending an unchanged value, which is the window module's business and nobody else's.
onOcrLine's job shrinks to routing. Where it previously reached into the BrowserWindow — checking visibility, re-applying collection behaviour after showing, deduplicating the offset, hashing the cover list — it now says trackTarget(frame, covers) and lets the panel decide. Same code, one caller.
Two small things fixed in passing, both safe: noteActivity took a `win` parameter it never used and which shadowed the module's own, and the retarget path in cfg:save open-coded what is now reset().
Verified: 35 assertions green, and a five-second Electron smoke run that reached a real capture — [win] shown, [win] target frame, [win] covered by 0 window(s), [ocr] emitted — so trackTarget was exercised end to end rather than merely parsed.
* refactor: permissions and the tray move out; main.js becomes wiring
main.js 361 -> 245 lines, and module-scope mutable state 4 -> ZERO. It now requires its parts, connects them, and handles shutdown.
permissions.js owns the two grants and reports them. They fail differently, which is the reason both are checked: without Screen Recording nothing works at all, while without Accessibility the global trigger silently never fires and the log stays clean. reportSpawnFailure joins them — a missing binary is the third thing that can be wrong with the environment, and blaming Screen Recording for it sends the user to the wrong settings pane.
tray.js reads permissions rather than being handed their state, and takes its two actions as handlers. That keeps the dependency one-way: permissions knows nothing about the tray, and notifies through a callback main supplies.
Verified: 35 assertions green, plus a five-second Electron run reaching app ready, tray built, both children started, deinflector loaded and trigger config pushed to the renderer.
* chore: trim the split's overhead, and rewrite CONVENTIONS for the new shape
Splitting one file into twenty-five buys per-file overhead. Some of that is unavoidable; a lot of it was mine.
- Swift imports: every extracted file got all six imports of the original. Now each takes only what it uses — 128 import lines down to 64. - The "Split from the original single-file OCR helper" line was repeated in 22 files. Git records that; the files do not need to. - Four JS module headers were 12-16 lines of archaeology about which variables used to live in main.js. That belongs in the commit message.
Swift 3173 -> 3057 with the build and golden-master unchanged.
CONVENTIONS.md is rewritten rather than patched. The principles were the good part and are kept verbatim — measure don't infer, no per-app special cases, degrade honestly, cite the measurement, delete the mechanism. What changed:
- "Single file, no package manifest" was simply false. Replaced with the rule that actually holds: one file per pipeline stage, a glob build, no Package.swift, and the fact that `private` no longer reaches across files. - Testing was one paragraph about the heavy suites. It is now the three tiers with what each can and cannot see, plus the rule this refactor ran on: record golden before a structural change, require byte-identical after. - Added the two module shapes that now exist (main-process modules taking their dependencies as arguments; renderer IIFEs exposing one window namespace, because classic scripts share a global scope and load order is load-bearing), and the layout rule that one file per language knows where things are. - Added "move code, or change code — never both", which governed every commit on this branch. - Corrected a gotcha that was wrong: Electron CAN be driven from a plain shell, including a hidden window with real Chromium layout. That is how the renderer suite runs. What cannot be scripted is the packaged .app and its TCC prompts. - Added two things measured the hard way this session: nothing but the loader may live in app/shell/, and mapfile is bash 4 while macOS ships 3.2.
* feat: validate everything crossing the IPC boundary
CONVENTIONS says to treat everything crossing IPC as untrusted. Nothing did. `lookup` forwarded whatever arrived into a prefix-scanning query loop, and `cfg:save` merged an arbitrary object into the file that supplies the capture child's argv.
This is not defence against a hostile renderer — it runs our own code behind contextIsolation and a sandbox. It is defence against a BUG in that code arriving as a shape nobody expected, which is the failure that costs an afternoon because it surfaces three layers away from its cause.
ipc.js all seven handlers in one place, with structural guards, and a one-line complaint per channel the first time one is rejected. A silently ignored message is exactly what costs the afternoon. config.js sanitize() clamps the values that reach argv: bundle id, window id, modifier, mode, hover delay, engine, interval, vote counts, dictionary entries. Unknown keys pass through untouched so the settings window can grow without this function knowing first. tier2.js the crop request must be finite numbers within plausible bounds; a NaN became a crop command the watch process cannot parse.
spawn() is called with an argv array and no shell, so none of this was a command-injection risk. What it prevents is a malformed setting producing a child that exits with a usage error the user then has to trace back to a settings field.
Eight new assertions cover sanitize(), including that every real modifier is accepted — a whitelist that rejects a legitimate value is worse than none.
Also verified, and now recorded rather than assumed: the renderer really is sandboxed. A probe with the panel's exact webPreferences reports process.sandboxed === true and require('fs') failing in the preload. PLAN.md Stage 6's "sandbox: true where possible" was already satisfied by Electron's defaults; no code was needed.
main.js is 224 lines and holds no ipcMain call at all.
Found by the Electron smoke run, not by review: ipc.register() was placed before eventsChild was declared, and threw on load. node --check cannot see that.
* docs: an index, an accurate architecture map, and the finished plans archived
docs/ had grown to seven files with no way to tell which mattered, and 1125 of its 2509 lines were plans for work that is now done.
README.md new. What each doc is for and when to read it, plus the five things worth knowing if you read nothing else. history/ REFACTOR and REFACTOR-INTEGRATION move here, each with a header saying it describes the codebase BEFORE the restructure. They are kept for the reasoning — the sourced findings and the measurement behind each decision are why the current shape is what it is — not as instructions.
ARCHITECTURE's file table listed seven files, three of which no longer hold what it claimed. Replaced with a tree of where things actually live and a table that points at the pieces, each cross-referenced to the load-bearing decision it implements. The nine decisions themselves are untouched: they are still true and still the most valuable thing in the repo.
INTEGRATION kept nine references of the form KindleOCR.swift:1070 into a file that no longer exists. Repointed at the files that hold that code now. The line numbers are gone for good, which is fine — they were stale before the restructure too.
PLAN now records the structure and testing work as done, marks the Stage 6 security item done with what was actually measured, and carries forward the two things the restructure deliberately did NOT do: the phantom-typed rects (with the live hazard spelled out) and a smoke test for the four CLI paths golden cannot see. Both were only findable inside a 673-line plan document before; they are now in the file people read to decide what to work on.
* ci: build the Swift helper, run the unit tests, check the conventions
Two jobs, both free on a public repo.
checks (ubuntu) node --check / bash -n / py_compile over everything, the two unit suites that need no generated data, shellcheck, and tools/check-conventions.sh swift (macos) ocr/build.sh — compiling IS the check — plus the four CLI paths the golden harness structurally cannot see
check-conventions.sh enforces the rules from CONVENTIONS that a machine can: nothing but the loader in app/shell (electron-packager copies that directory wholesale into the signed bundle), no directory resolved outside paths.js, no module-scope mutable state in main.js, nodeIntegration never enabled, no unsafe-inline back in the renderer CSP, every doc link resolving, and no bash 4 builtins — macOS ships 3.2, and mapfile fails at run time rather than parse time, so nothing else catches it. Each one is a mistake that either happened during this refactor or would quietly undo something the design depends on.
Two things deliberately NOT in CI:
lookup.test.js needs data/index.db, ~370 MB and generated. golden.sh needs test/gt/ AND is machine-local by nature: Vision's model version differs between macOS releases, so a byte-exact baseline recorded on a laptop cannot be reproduced on a runner. It stays a local pre-commit gate, which is what it was designed as.
Writing the checks turned up three false positives in my own first draft — node_modules unexcluded, the CSP check matching the comment that says "no unsafe-inline", and the bash 4 check matching its own explanation. Fixed; worth recording that a convention checker needs testing like anything else.
Dependabot watches Electron monthly, since a major bump changes the bundled Node that node:sqlite comes from and can change sandbox defaults.
* docs: rewrite the README in a human voice
It read like it was generated, because in large part it was. Rewritten to sound like someone describing their own project: first person where that is honest, contractions, plainer sentences, fewer em-dashes (20 -> 9), and tables turned back into prose or plain lists where a table was never earning anything. 203 lines down to 121 saying the same things.
Dropped the vocabulary that gave it away — "load-bearing" above all, which appeared here and still appears four times in the docs where it is actually carrying meaning.
Two factual fixes while rewriting:
- The configuration section documented trigger.mode as "hover" and hoverDelayMs as 70. Those are one machine's settings, not the shipped defaults, which config.js sets to "hold" and 250. This was wrong before the rewrite too. - The file/path table listed app/renderer/index.html as owning the glyph layer and hit-testing, which stopped being true when the renderer was split. Replaced with a sentence about the actual layout.
I also cut an origin story the draft invented — a first-person account of why the project was started is not mine to write. There is a natural place for one in the opening if you want it.
* ci: fix the two shellcheck warnings in check-conventions.sh
The conventions checker failed the check it exists to run, which is fitting.
SC2164 cd "$PROJECT_ROOT" without || exit. A failed cd would have run every check against whatever directory the runner happened to be in, and reported a pass. SC2010 ls | grep to list app/shell. Breaks on filenames with newlines or leading dashes; find does the filtering itself.
Both fixed rather than suppressed — a warning waived in the first week is a warning waived forever. The Swift job passed on macos-latest, so the helper compiles on a clean machine as well as this one.</pre>

entry.title: Hide the overlay when the target window is not visible
entry.content:
Hide the overlay when the target window is not visible

The panel joins every Space so it can float over a reader in native
fullscreen, so swiping to another desktop carried the glyph layer and any
open popup along with you and left them sitting on top of whatever was
there. Nothing hid it for up to 8s — and nothing hid it at all when another
window simply came up over the reader: capture excludes every other window,
so a buried target still yields pristine pixels and looks exactly like one
being read.

- chooseWindow() subtracts the ordinary windows (layer 0, not transparent)
  the window server composites in FRONT of a candidate before applying the
  existing "≥50% visible" test, so a buried window is no longer "on screen".
- stillVisible() re-runs that test from CGWindowList alone — 0.5ms, no
  SCShareableContent, no capture — and the watch loop asks it every 150ms
  while it waits out the interval. Measured 0.15s from the target
  disappearing to the idle marker, against 0.7s for the next heartbeat and
  1.3s for the next OCR pass.
- main.js hides on that marker immediately instead of waiting out
  IDLE_HIDE_MS (now only the backstop for a watcher gone silent), and tells
  the renderer to drop the popup with it.
- Partial cover is not a reason to hide — half a page is still readable — so
  payloads and heartbeats carry the covered regions frame-local as `covers`.
  The renderer refuses lookups inside them and drops a popup whose word has
  just been buried.

Display bounds in that path come from CGDisplayBounds, not NSScreen: it runs
off the main thread every 150ms, and NSScreen.frame is bottom-left-origin,
which agrees with a window rect only on one display at 0,0.

Measured with a two-window rig: target off the on-screen list ⟹ idle in
0.15s; fully covered ⟹ no window reported; cover over the right half ⟹ still
tracked, covers [{400,0,400×600}]; cover in a corner ⟹ [{580,180,220×300}];
cover moved away ⟹ []. Selection still follows z-order in both directions.

entry.title: Yomi Overlay: Yomitan-style popup dictionary over any macOS window
entry.content:
Yomi Overlay: Yomitan-style popup dictionary over any macOS window

ScreenCaptureKit + Vision/Live Text OCR of a single target window, an
invisible per-glyph text layer positioned over the real pixels, and
Yomitan's own deinflector against a SQLite index built from Yomitan
dictionary zips.

Handles horizontal and vertical Japanese including mixed pages, strips
furigana from the pixels before recognition, and majority-votes across
re-reads of a static page.

Paths are derived rather than written down so a clone works outside the
original checkout. Dictionary data, the built index, and the ground-truth
corpora are not redistributed — setup.sh fetches or regenerates them.
